paper.title: RETHINKING THE ROLE OF FRAMES FOR SE(3)-INVARIANT CRYSTAL STRUCTURE MODELING
paper.research_summary: This paper proposes dynamic frames for SE(3)-invariant crystal structure modeling, challenging the conventional use of static frames. Dynamic frames are constructed per atom and per message-passing layer using learned attention weights to capture local interatomic interactions, rather than aligning with the global static structure. The concept is implemented in CrystalFramer, a transformer-based architecture extending Crystalformer, and evaluated on crystal property prediction tasks across JARVIS, Materials Project, and OQMD datasets.

task.objective: Predict material properties (e.g., formation energy, bandgap) from crystal structures while maintaining SE(3) invariance.
input_requirements: crystal structure represented as unit cell (A, P, L)

evidence.text: To validate the effectiveness of the proposed dynamic frames, we conducted extensive experiments on crystal property prediction.

We use three datasets: JARVIS (55,723 materials), MP (69,239 materials), and OQMD (817,636 materials), using snapshots available through a Python package (jarvis-tools). These datasets provide several material properties, such as formation energy and bandgap, simulated by DFT calculations.
Tables 1 and 2 extensively compare the mean absolute errors of the proposed and existing methods for the JARVIS (5 tasks) and MP (4 tasks) datasets.

stages.stage_goal: Train the CrystalFramer model using Adam optimizer and inverse square root learning rate scheduling.

evidence.text: For the JARVIS dataset, we train our model from scratch by optimizing the mean absolute loss function using Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) for a total of 2000 epochs, while enabling the frames from the beginning.

We employ the warm-up-free inverse square root scheduling (Huang et al., 2020) for the learning rate, with the initial learning rate of 5.0 × 10−4 and decay factor of √4000/(4000 + t) according to the total train steps t.
